## Where it comes from

Two parallel streams of flowing water — one of the script's classic
pictures, already recognizable in the earliest tablets. It writes
the word *a*, "water," and because Sumerian used the bare sound /a/
everywhere — in names, in grammar — the water sign became the
script's busiest syllable: the rebus leap of
<a href="{{ '/cuneiform/101/03-how-signs-mean/' | relative_url }}">101's chapter 03</a>
in its purest form.

## How to remember it

**Water** runs in two thin channels, side by side — two long wedges
like irrigation ditches seen from the air. Everything in Sumer
begins with water in a channel; so does the sign list.

## In the wild

  <div class="reading-lines">
    <div class="reading-line"><span class="script">𒀀𒈬𒈾𒊒</span><span class="translit">a mu-na-ru</span><span class="gloss">"dedicated this to him"</span></div>
  </div>
  <figcaption class="citation">
    Votive inscription, Uruk, late third millennium BCE.
    <a href="https://cdli.earth/artifacts/216758">CDLI P216758</a>
    via Nabu, <code>urn:nabu:cdli:p216758</code> · license:
    attribution.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

Piece by piece:

- **a** — the object slot of the formula, compressed to one vowel
- **mu-na-ru** — the verb chain: *mu-* "did," *-na-* "for him,"
  *ru* "dedicate"

The closing words of a thousand votive gifts — and the water sign
opens them sounding as plain /a/, no water in sight. The whole
formula is taken apart in
<a href="{{ '/cuneiform/102/12-the-chain-completed/' | relative_url }}">102's chapter 12</a>.
